math.title: A passing Judge score did not guarantee clean supervision
math.description: Independent Review found 45 core defects among 270 reviewed selections from C1/P1, despite all 384 passing the selection Judge. C1/P2 added a fresh blind verification pass while holding the mixture and length controls fixed.
math.quote: Independent selected-example Review nevertheless found that 45 of 270 usable normalized rows failed at least one core axis

math.title: Saturated scores motivated a more discriminating selector
math.description: C3/P1 assigned the maximum score to 2,888 candidates, yet reviewed selections still contained errors and repetitive reasoning. C3/P2 replaced that coarse score with task-aware validity checks and a ranking of useful progress.
math.quote: It assigned the maximum projected score to 2,888 candidates

math.title: Inspect repetition directly
math.description: Review linked repetition to major errors in C3/P2. C3/P3 still contained repeated paragraphs after two semantic checks. C1/P4 therefore tested a deterministic repeated-span filter while retaining the leader’s length bands.
math.quote: direct deterministic inspection of stored response text can expose repetition that saturated semantic labels miss

math.title: Separate evidence coverage from shorter training targets
math.description: C3/P2 lacked matched Judge evidence for 23 selected pairs. C3/P3 showed that exact-pair binding was feasible, but also shortened the training targets. C3/P4 isolated exact-pair assessment while restoring the leader’s length and exposure controls.
math.quote: only 361 of its 384 stored question/response pairs have matched completed task-aware assessment evidence

math.title: Repair the known gaps instead of selecting everything again
math.description: C3/P4 repaired evidence coverage but lost five solved problems relative to C3/P2. C3/P5 proposed retaining the 361 already assessed leader selections and replacing only the 23 unmatched pairs.
math.quote: Neither tests retaining the 361 already supported leader members and changing only the known evidence failures

math.title: Change how verification obtains its reference
math.description: Both earlier verification attempts still admitted flawed responses and reduced validation scores. C1/P5 proposed creating a reference without seeing the candidate answer, rather than repeating the same answer-conditioned verification.
math.quote: They do not test a reference created without exposure to the candidate answer

reward.title: Relative quality can still reward an unsound answer
reward.description: C1/P1 made group rewards more varied, but 16.80% of training rows were verifier-wrong and received positive advantage. C1/P2 added an absolute quality requirement before rewarding failed responses.
reward.quote: Population evidence shows that 16.80% of all rows were verifier-wrong but received positive realized advantage

reward.title: Require support from other responses in the group
reward.description: C1/P2’s promoted responses were much less reliable when supporting process evidence was sparse. C1/P3 made credit for an all-wrong group depend on corroboration from multiple sibling responses.
reward.quote: 134 of 193 promoted rows were incorrect when support was sparse, versus 22 of 129 when support was broad

reward.title: A hard support threshold discards useful boundary cases
reward.description: Review found useful mathematical work just below C1/P3’s corroboration threshold, where every response received zero credit. C1/P4 tested relative process credit near that boundary.
reward.quote: a hard sibling-corroboration cliff discards task-aligned relative evidence immediately below its eligibility boundary

reward.title: Withdraw credit from weakly supported groups
reward.description: The relaxed branch in C1/P4 gave positive advantage to 201 verifier-wrong responses in the reviewed sample; 140 were substantively wrong. C1/P5 restricted positive credit to strongly corroborated groups.
reward.quote: Of 201 outcome-failed responses that received positive actual advantage there, 140 were substantively wrong

reward.title: Relevance is weaker evidence than a sound derivation
reward.description: C3/P1’s progress ranking often agreed with Review, but 239 of 678 reviewed wrong responses with positive advantage made no mathematical progress. C3/P2 prioritized derivational and conclusion support over relevance.
reward.quote: 239 (`35.3%`) were independently judged to show no mathematical progress

reward.title: Use successful siblings to anchor process credit
reward.description: C3/P2 still promoted unsupported responses in all-wrong groups. C2/P1 supplied a contrasting example with no positive advantage for outcome-failed rows. C3/P3 combined progress discrimination with an outcome-success anchor.
reward.quote: it recorded no positive advantage for any outcome-failed row

reward.title: Check whether a successful answer is a sound anchor
reward.description: C3/P3’s reviews exposed flawed reasoning in some outcome-correct answers. C2/P2 showed that process evidence could distinguish stronger and weaker successful responses. C3/P4 required process support before a successful sibling could anchor credit.
reward.quote: outcome success does not make all successful responses equally credible as reasoning anchors

reward.title: Keep useful process ordering without the unsafe all-wrong branch
reward.description: C1/P3 showed useful within-outcome ordering but also false positive winners in all-wrong groups. C3/P3 preserved negative advantage for every verifier-wrong row. C2/P5 proposed combining the safer mixed-group behavior with process ordering in all-successful groups.
reward.quote: The second source left all-successful groups at identity
